newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says latest U.N. resolution "unacceptable".
newsitem.headline: Iraq says latest U.N. resolution "unacceptable".

text.p: Iraq's leadership rejected a U.N. resolution threatening Baghdad with further sanctions if it obstructed arms inspectors and said the step was unjustified.

A statement published by Iraqi newspapers on Monday after an Iraqi Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) meeting chaired by President Saddam Hussein late on Sunday said the latest United Nations Security Council resolution had "disregarded all facts and cannot be accepted by any fair-minded people throughout the world".
The Council on Saturday unanimously warned Iraq it would face further sanctions if it did not allow U.N. arms inspectors to search sensitive sites.

Iraq's prevention of inspections of three sites this month prompted Rolf Ekeus, chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of dismantling Iraq's prohibited weapons, to complain to the council last week.

The RCC said Iraq had met all its commitments toward the U.N. resolutions which governed the ceasefire of the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait and it was high time for the council to lift the sanctions imposed for Baghdad's 1990 invasion of its neighbour.
"We demand in clear terms and words that the Security Council...embarks on the total and comprehensive lifting of the sanctions," it said.

UNSCOM must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on its oil exports. The U.N. has allowed Baghdad since December to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy urgently needed goods.

The RCC statement accused the United States of being behind the new U.N. resolution, saying: "America wants to delay the implementation of what should be carried out by the Security Council toward its obligations".
In New York, Iraq's Deputy Premier Tareq Aziz described the resolution as "the outcome of American fabrication in which Rolf Ekeus has took part".

The official newspaper al-Qadissiya declared that the new resolution was taken "to give the Special Commission wider powers in order to commit provocative acts against Iraq and to threaten Iraq's sovereignty".

Deputy chairman of UNSCOM Charles Duelfer has been meeting with senior Iraqi officials in Baghdad since Saturday. He said Iraq was still concealing weapons of mass destruction but Baghdad has denied the charge.
